metaDescription: Four genuine Milwaukee cordless vacuums for M12 and M18 owners, compared on tank size, water lift, noise and bare-tool cost, with notes on what is handheld.
expertTake: The M12 FUEL 1.6-gallon wet/dry vacuum is the best Milwaukee pick for most owners because it is the most portable and stackable of the four. The M18 VC2-0 is the quiet, mid-size choice for occupied rooms. Anyone who wants a true pistol-grip hand vacuum should be aware that none of these are one, and look at the brands that make them.
introParagraphs: This is a tool brand, and its vacuums follow tool logic: they run on the same battery families that already power a crew's drills and saws, and they are sold as bare tools more often than as kits. What they are not is a household dustbuster, with a pistol grip and a wall charger.

That matters for the word handheld in the search. The four machines here are compact cordless wet/dry vacuums carried by a handle, and they sit one size above a true hand vac. If that suits you, the choice is mostly about tank size, battery platform and how loud the motor is, and the sections below compare those points in turn.

products.name: Milwaukee 0960-20 M12 FUEL 1.6-gallon wet/dry vacuum, tool only
products.description:
The 0960-20 is the most compact and portable of the four, and that is why it comes first. A 1.6-gallon tank sits on the M12 battery, which is a smaller, lighter pack than the M18, so the whole machine is easier to carry up a ladder, into a van or under a sink. The listing describes a stackable design with onboard accessory storage, which fits it into a tool system.

A brushless motor in the FUEL line runs cooler and wastes less energy, and the listing quotes a 42 inch water lift, which is a pressure figure that hints at real lifting power for wet debris. Compared with the M18 FPOVCL it is smaller and lighter, and compared with the older M18 0880-20 it is more modern in motor design.

It is a tool-only listing, so battery and charger cost extra unless you already own M12 packs. After wet use, empty and rinse the tank and let it dry with the lid off. Wash the filter when airflow drops. A second listing of the same machine appears as vacuum-only, so treat the two as one product when you compare prices. The stackable design is a quiet advantage in a van, because the tank locks onto a tool case and does not slide when you brake. Because the pack sits on top, it is also the easiest of the four to swap without tipping the tank.
products.bestFor: M12 owners who want the most portable Milwaukee wet/dry vacuum.
pros: Compact 1.6-gallon tank on the light M12 battery
cons: Tool only, battery and charger extra

products.name: Milwaukee M18 VC2-0 compact wet/dry vacuum, 7.5 liters, tool only
products.description:
The VC2-0 is the compact M18 option, and its listing puts the noise at 69 decibels, which is low for a shop-style vacuum and useful in an occupied office, a client's kitchen or a hotel room. A listing noise figure is not an independent measurement, but the gap to the 87 dB quoted for the FPOVCL is large enough to matter.

A 7.5 liter tank is a little under two gallons, so it holds more than a true hand vac and less than the FPOVCL. It runs on the M18 battery family, which is the largest in the brand's line, so crews already on that system get a vacuum without a second charger ecosystem. It is carried by handle, and it is not a one-hand tool.

It is a tool-only listing, so budget for a pack if you have none. Empty the tank after wet work and let it dry with the lid off. Wash the filter when airflow drops, and check the hose for splits at the flex. It is the better choice than the M12 FUEL if you already own M18 packs and want a quieter machine, and the worse one if weight matters. A quiet machine changes how you work, because you can run it while someone is on a phone call or a patient is in the next chair. For a service technician who cleans up after every call, that courtesy is worth more than a bigger tank.
products.bestFor: M18 owners who work in occupied rooms and want a quieter vacuum.

products.name: Milwaukee M18 FPOVCL 2.5-gallon cordless wet/dry vacuum
products.description:
The FPOVCL has the largest tank of the four at 2.5 gallons, which puts it nearer a small shop vacuum than a handheld. A listed 47 inch water lift and a claim of up to 70 percent more suction than an earlier model describe a stronger motor, though the 800 W figure is a motor rating, not a measure of cleaning ability.

It is the machine for a crew that clears a whole room of debris each day and wants one tank to hold it all. The trade is noise and weight: the listing quotes 87 decibels, far louder than the VC2-0, and a tank of wet debris is heavy to carry. Choose it over the compact units only when tank size is your limit.

Wet pickup demands a drained and rinsed tank at the end of the day. Wipe the filter cage, keep the hose free of kinks and empty at about half full on liquids. A larger pack suits the larger motor, so do not pair it with the smallest battery in the toolbox. It is a sensible choice for a renovation crew that sweeps a room before the painters arrive, and a poor choice for a technician who climbs a ladder with a vacuum in one hand. If you are unsure which tank you need, the 7.5 liter VC2-0 fills most jobs and the FPOVCL only pays off when you routinely overflow it.
products.bestFor: Crews that need the largest cordless Milwaukee tank.

products.name: Milwaukee 0880-20 18-volt cordless wet/dry vacuum
products.description:
The 0880-20 is the older design, and its main selling point is compatibility. The listing says it works on all Milwaukee 18V slide-on batteries, lithium-ion or NiCd, so a crew with a drawer of older packs can put them to use instead of buying new ones.

It has no brushless motor and no published water-lift or noise figure in the listing, so it is the hardest to compare on paper. It sits behind the FPOVCL and the M12 FUEL for engineering, and it is the choice only when legacy packs are the point. A used or old-stock unit may also arrive with a worn gasket or an aged filter.

Inspect the seals and replace the filter on arrival. Empty and rinse the tank after wet work and dry it with the lid off. If you are starting from zero, buy a current M12 or M18 machine instead. Older slide-on packs lose capacity with age, so test them on a short job before relying on one for a long clean-up. A NiCd pack in particular has a memory effect and a higher self-discharge rate than a modern lithium cell, so expect shorter runs from it.
products.bestFor: Owners with a stock of older 18V Milwaukee batteries.
pros: Uses packs you may already own

buyingCriteria.explanation: The M12 FUEL 0960-20 runs on the smaller, lighter M12 pack, while the VC2-0 and FPOVCL run on the larger M18. Buy the machine that matches the batteries you already own, because a pack and charger are the costly part. Do not mix up the two systems, since the packs are not interchangeable. A crew that runs both can carry one charger of each and rotate packs through the day, but a household owner is better off picking the single platform that matches their drill. If you own neither, M12 is the cheaper route in and M18 the broader one.

The 0960-20's 1.6 gallons, the VC2-0's 7.5 liters and the FPOVCL's 2.5 gallons span a real range. A bigger tank saves trips to the drain but adds weight when full, especially with liquid. Choose the smallest that fits your usual job. A wet tank is heavy, since water weighs about eight pounds a gallon, so a nominal 2.5 gallons is never fully usable on liquid. Stop at about two thirds full on wet work, and pour out before you carry the unit up stairs.

The VC2-0 lists 69 dB and the FPOVCL 87 dB, a gap of 18 dB on a logarithmic scale. A loud machine is a problem in offices and clinics. Treat listing figures as a guide, not as a lab result. A machine that is 18 dB quieter sounds roughly a quarter as loud to most listeners, so the gap is far bigger than it looks on paper. If you work around clients, patients or sleeping children, that is the spec to weigh most heavily.

A listed water lift such as the 0960-20's 42 inches or the FPOVCL's 47 inches indicates lifting pressure. A brushless FUEL motor runs cooler and lasts longer. Watts and horsepower on a box are less informative than these. Water lift tells you how well the machine pulls on a stuck load such as wet debris in a deep hose, while airflow tells you how fast it moves light dust. Neither is printed as a sustained figure, so treat both as a guide.

All four listings are tool-only or near it. A battery and charger can cost as much as the vacuum itself. Count that before comparing prices with a kit. If you already own a handful of packs for other tools, a bare tool is the cheapest route, and a kit would leave you with duplicates. If you own none, a corded shop vacuum may be the better value than a cordless one.

These are compact wet/dry vacuums carried by a handle, not pistol-grip handhelds. If you want a one-hand tool for shelves, look at a different brand's hand vac. If you want volume, a Milwaukee tank unit fits.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform and portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared M12 and M18 designs and body weight. The 0960-20 led for portability and the FPOVCL for capacity. Fit to your batteries decided ties.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and lift
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at brushless motors and listed water lift. The FUEL machine and the FPOVCL led. The 0880-20 trailed on published detail.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the listed decibel figures, 69 dB for the VC2-0 and 87 dB for the FPOVCL. Quiet machines scored for indoor work. Figures are listing claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tank and weight
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 1.6-gallon, 7.5-liter and 2.5-gallon tanks against carry weight. Smaller was better for ladders, bigger for rooms.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We read owner feedback patterns on filter clogging, latch durability and battery cost, weighing the recurring complaints over one-off reviews. Milwaukee tools draw praise for build and criticism for bare-tool cost. Price tier ordered the lineup only, and no price figures are quoted in this guide.

cards.label: M12
cards.text: The 0960-20 runs on the lighter pack and is easier to carry. It has a smaller tank and the pack runs a shorter time.

cards.label: M18
cards.text: The VC2-0 and FPOVCL run on the larger pack and hold more. They weigh more and need an M18 charger.

howToChoose.note: Pick M12 if you work on ladders and in tight spaces, and M18 if you already own those batteries.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a wet rating, a washable filter and a tank you can empty and rinse quickly. A float shutoff is a bonus.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The M18 VC2-0 and FPOVCL both list wet and dry use, and the 0960-20 adds the portable M12 option.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more on the FPOVCL or 0960-20 if you clean weekly on site. Tool-grade motors and tanks earn the premium.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save with the VC2-0 or 0880-20 if you already own the packs. A cheaper machine is fine for occasional use.

maintenance.why: Liquid left in a tank smells and corrodes metal parts and the filter cage. Rinse it and let it dry with the lid off so air can circulate.
A clogged filter is the main cause of weak suction, and fine drywall dust clogs it fast. Dry it fully before refit so the foam does not smell or grow mould.
Hoses split at the flex and latches pick up grit from jobsite dust. Replace a cracked hose or a loose latch early, because a leak at either one cuts suction and can pull dust past the filter.
An aged gasket leaks air and cuts suction, which is common on older or old-stock machines. Replace worn seals before you blame the motor or the battery.
Lithium packs fade when hot or empty, and a truck dashboard in summer is hot. Keep them indoors at partial charge and rotate them so no single pack does all the work.

faq.q: Does Milwaukee make a true handheld vacuum?
faq.a: The machines in this guide are compact cordless wet/dry vacuums carried by a handle. A pistol-grip hand vac is a different type, so check the model before you buy, and read the listing for the words handheld, wet or dry and tool only so there is no surprise on delivery.

They are tool-only or near it. Plan to buy a pack and charger if you do not already own the matching M12 or M18 system, and size the pack to the job, since a larger battery runs a vacuum noticeably longer than a compact one.

faq.q: What about vacuums made for Milwaukee batteries?
faq.a: Those are third-party products sold as compatible with Milwaukee packs. They are not Milwaukee machines and are not ranked here, and their warranty and support come from an unrelated seller, so read the terms carefully if you consider one.

The M18 VC2-0 lists 69 dB, much lower than the FPOVCL's 87 dB. Treat listing figures as guides, not lab results, but the gap is wide enough that the VC2-0 is the safer choice for indoor jobs near people, and the FPOVCL is better kept for sites where hearing protection is already worn.

Yes, they are listed as wet/dry. Empty and dry the tank and filter after wet use, and never use them on petrol, solvents, hot ash or embers, because a standard motor can spark. Stay below about two thirds full on liquid so the float and motor stay protected.

M12 is lighter and more portable, M18 is bigger and holds more. Match the machine to the batteries you already own, since the pack and charger are the costly part of any cordless tool. If you are choosing from scratch, think about your other tools first and let the vacuum follow.
